title: The plot
hookLine: the Meccan leaders plan to kill him with a man from every clan

lines: WHAT DO WE DO ABOUT HIM?
cards: Mecca is emptying out. House after house of believers stands locked, the owners gone north to Yathrib, where they now have protectors. The leaders of Quraysh can see where this is heading.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is still in the city, with Abu Bakr and Ali. If he joins the others, he'll be out of reach, among people sworn to defend him. So they meet in the council house, the Dar al-Nadwa.
One question on the table: what do we do about him? Today: the plot.

teach.h: LOCK HIM UP, OR DRIVE HIM OUT?
teach.b: Ibn Ishaq records the debate. One voice says: lock him up in irons and wait for him to die, as poets have died before. No, says another: his followers will hear and come to free him.
Drive him out, then, and we'll be rid of him. No: look how sweet his speech is, how he wins hearts. He'll gather an army and come back.
Then Abu Jahl gives the plan they choose.

teach.h: A YOUNG MAN FROM EVERY CLAN.
teach.b: Take one strong young man from every clan, give each a sharp sword, and let them strike him all at once, like a single man.
His blood will be spread across all the clans, his family can't fight everyone, and they'll have to take blood money instead.
It's a cold plan, and clever: everyone's crime, so no one's. Ibn Ishaq adds a strange detail.
The voice that knocked down prison and exile, and praised the killing, belonged to an old man from Najd who had joined the meeting, and Ibn Ishaq says he was Iblis, Satan, in disguise.
What the Qur'an says about that night is short. It reminds the Prophet of when those who disbelieved plotted against him, to hold him captive, or kill him, or drive him out.
They plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of planners.
In the common reading, the verse lists the same three options the council argued over: captivity, killing, exile. And it doesn't describe a counter-army. It just sets their planning beside God's.

how: Muslims recite the verse about this plot (8:30) and retell the night of the council when they remember the hijra, often as a reminder to trust God's planning over their own.

o: a plan to drive him out of Mecca for good
Quraysh's plan to kill him, one man per clan
a plan to lock him in irons until he died

a young man from every clan

with his followers gone north, he'd soon be beyond their reach.

games.q: you sit on the council. someone proposes exile: just drive him out. what does the room decide?
o: kill him with a man from every clan.
games.why: they rejected prison and exile, and chose Abu Jahl's plan. the Qur'an answers: they plotted, and God plotted.

practice: Bring to mind something you're anxious about: a decision others are making about you, a meeting, a diagnosis, a person who seems set against you, and notice how much of the planning is out of your hands.

Then remember that the story doesn't end with the council's vote. If you pray, you can ask God for protection in your own words, or with a line you know from the Qur'an; if you don't, simply breathe out the part you can't control.

wordCard.voice: The plot. Quraysh planned to kill the Prophet with a man from every clan, and the Qur'an sets their plotting beside God's. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: plotting, scheming; the word the Qur'an uses for both their plan and God's.

carryVoice: Your line: they planned; Allah planned. There were two plans that night, not one. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (Quraysh meet in Dar al-Nadwa; proposals to imprison or exile; Abu Jahl's plan of a young man from every clan; the old man of Najd)
